canonical_name: Young 1805 — An Essay on the Cohesion of Fluids
creator: Thomas Young
disclosure_citation: Young, T. (1805). 'An essay on the cohesion of fluids.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London 95: 65-87. doi:10.1098/rstl.1805.0005
notable_capabilities: mechanical theory of capillarity from solid-liquid-vapor force balance
Young equation gamma_sv = gamma_sl + gamma_lv cos(theta)
first formal definition of contact angle
notes: Foundational classical anchor; predates by two centuries any modern microfluidic patent on surface-energy-controlled flow.
prior_art_notes: Discloses the fundamental force balance at the three-phase (solid-liquid-vapor) contact line and defines the equilibrium contact angle in terms of the three interfacial tensions. This Young equation is the load-bearing relation for: (a) capillary-driven priming of microfluidic channels (paper microfluidics, lateral-flow assays, capillary stop valves); (b) all surface-treatment patents that claim a contact angle range to control wettability; (c) electrowetting devices (which modulate cos(theta) electrically — Lippmann's later equation reduces to a perturbation of Young); (d) hydrophilic/hydrophobic patterning to direct droplet motion. Anticipates any patent claim that recites 'controlling fluid motion by surface energy difference', 'directional flow by contact angle gradient', or 'stop valve formed by hydrophobic boundary' — Young 1805 published the underlying equation in the open literature 220 years prior. Particularly invalidates over-broad surface-energy-control claims that fail to disclose specific non-obvious geometries.

canonical_name: Laplace 1806 — Mecanique Celeste Supplement on Capillary Action
creator: Pierre-Simon Laplace
disclosure_citation: Laplace, P. S. (1806). 'Sur l'action capillaire,' Supplement to Book X of Traite de Mecanique Celeste, Vol. IV. Courcier, Paris. English: Bowditch translation, 1839, vol. IV.
notable_capabilities: derivation of capillary pressure jump Delta P = gamma (1/R1 + 1/R2)
treatment of meniscus shape via differential geometry of curved interfaces
extension of Young 1805 contact-angle physics to bulk pressure
notes: The single most-cited classical equation in microfluidic theory.
prior_art_notes: Discloses the Laplace pressure equation: the pressure difference across a curved fluid interface equals surface tension times mean curvature. Together with Young 1805 this forms the Young-Laplace equation, the universal governing relation for: (a) droplet pressure in T-junction and flow-focusing droplet generators; (b) bubble pinch-off and step emulsification; (c) capillary rise and capillary-driven priming in paper microfluidics; (d) Plateau-Rayleigh jet break-up; (e) the pressure threshold for breaking through a hydrophobic stop valve; (f) meniscus pinning at channel expansions and contractions; (g) the entire field of capillary stop valves on centrifugal microfluidic discs. Anticipates any claim that recites 'a pressure-balanced droplet generator', 'a capillary-pressure-driven valve', or 'a curved interface used to meter liquid' — Laplace 1806 published the governing equation 220 years before any microfluidic patent could have been filed.
sources: Laplace, Mecanique Celeste, Supplement to Book X (1806)
I. Newton & H. Bowditch facsimile editions

canonical_name: Young-Laplace Equation (combined 1805-1806)
creator: Thomas Young; Pierre-Simon Laplace
disclosure_citation: Young, T. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. 95, 65-87 (1805); Laplace, P. S. Mecanique Celeste, Supplement to Book X (1806). Combined as DeltaP = gamma(1/R1 + 1/R2) with boundary condition cos(theta) at three-phase line.
notable_capabilities: unified pressure-curvature-contact-angle theory of static capillarity
predicts capillary rise height
predicts droplet equilibrium shape under gravity (Bond number)
predicts critical pressure to push fluid through hydrophobic constriction
notes: Combined entry indexed as a single prior-art anchor for examiner search.
prior_art_notes: Combined Young-Laplace equation is the single most invoked classical result in microfluidic device design: every droplet generator, every capillary-driven assay, every paper-microfluidic device, and every surface-energy patterned channel inherits its quantitative behavior from this equation. As a unified prior-art anchor, the combined equation invalidates broad patents claiming 'surface-tension-driven actuation', 'capillary-pressure metering', 'bursting-pressure valve', 'pressure-controlled droplet sizing', and similar — the relation between curvature, pressure, and surface tension was published before electricity was understood as an EM phenomenon.
sources: Laplace Mecanique Celeste Supp. Book X (1806)
de Gennes, Brochard-Wyart, Quere 'Capillarity and Wetting Phenomena' (Springer 2003) Ch. 1

canonical_name: Hagen 1839 — On the motion of water in narrow cylindrical tubes (Hagen-Poiseuille flow)
creator: Gotthilf Heinrich Ludwig Hagen
disclosure_citation: G. Hagen, 'Über die Bewegung des Wassers in engen cylindrischen Röhren', Poggendorffs Annalen der Physik und Chemie 46, 423-442 (1839)
prior_art_notes: First quantitative experimental description of laminar pressure-driven flow in narrow cylindrical tubes, predating Poiseuille's 1840 publication. Establishes the fourth-power dependence of volumetric flow on tube radius (Hagen-Poiseuille law). Foundational for ALL pressure-driven microfluidic theory: every channel-resistance calculation, every flow-controller specification, every droplet-generator design implicitly relies on this 1839 disclosure. Anticipates: any patent that recites 'flow rate determined by pressure drop and channel hydraulic resistance' as part of its operating principle — the relation is 187 years old.
sources: Poggendorffs Annalen der Physik und Chemie vol 46 (1839)

canonical_name: Poiseuille 1840 — Experimental research on the motion of liquids in tubes of very small diameter
creator: Jean Léonard Marie Poiseuille
disclosure_citation: J.L.M. Poiseuille, 'Recherches expérimentales sur le mouvement des liquides dans les tubes de très petits diamètres', Comptes Rendus 11, 961-967 and 1041-1048 (1840); full memoir Mém. Savants Étrang. 9, 433-543 (1846)
prior_art_notes: Independent and more rigorous experimental establishment of pressure-driven laminar flow in capillary tubes; Poiseuille's name attaches to the law (Hagen-Poiseuille). For microfluidics, Poiseuille is the canonical 19th-century experimentalist demonstrating that the same physical relation governs flow in tubes from millimeter to capillary scale. Anticipates: any patent claim to a microfluidic 'channel of small diameter exhibiting laminar flow with parabolic velocity profile' as the operative physics; the parabolic profile in capillaries was experimentally established 1840.

canonical_name: Peclet Number Pe = U L / D
creator: Jean Claude Eugene Peclet (heat-transfer origin); standardized via mid-20th-c. transport texts
disclosure_citation: Peclet, J. C. E. (1841). 'Traite de la chaleur considerée dans ses applications.' Hachette, Paris (2nd ed., 3 vol.); dimensionless-group form codified in 20th-century transport literature.
notable_capabilities: Pe = U L / D — ratio of advective to diffusive transport
Pe = Re * Sc (mass) or Pe = Re * Pr (heat)
controls mixing time in laminar microchannels
prior_art_notes: Peclet number is the controlling parameter for every microfluidic mixer: at low Pe, diffusion dominates and mixing is fast; at high Pe (typical of microfluidics with small molecules at modest velocity), advection dominates and passive mixers like the Stroock 2002 staggered herringbone are required. Anchors: (a) all passive micromixer patents that recite mixing-length-vs-Peclet scaling; (b) Taylor-Aris dispersion analysis (combined with Aris 1956); (c) hydrodynamic focusing of analytes into a thin laminar stream for downstream detection. Any patent claim to 'mixing time scaling' or 'advection-dominated transport regime' is anticipated by the Peclet group.
sources: Peclet, J. C. E. 'Traite de la chaleur' (Hachette 1841)

canonical_name: Stokes 1851 — On the effect of internal friction of fluids on the motion of pendulums (Stokes drag, low-Re flow)
creator: George Gabriel Stokes
disclosure_citation: G.G. Stokes, 'On the effect of the internal friction of fluids on the motion of pendulums', Trans. Camb. Phil. Soc. 9, 8-106 (1851)
prior_art_notes: Foundational analysis of viscous flow at low Reynolds number; derives the Stokes drag formula F=6πµaU on a sphere — the canonical scaling for micro-particle motion in microfluidic channels. Anticipates: any patent that recites Stokes-drag-based separation, particle settling, or microbead capture in microfluidic flow as its operative physics. Required prior art for any 'particle separation by drag balance' claim. Also foundational for cell-handling microfluidics where Stokes drag balances against electrophoretic, dielectrophoretic, acoustic, or magnetic forces.

canonical_name: Darcy 1856 - Les Fontaines Publiques de la Ville de Dijon (Darcy's law)
creator: Henry Darcy
disclosure_citation: Darcy, H. (1856). 'Les Fontaines Publiques de la Ville de Dijon.' Victor Dalmont, Paris. Appendix D: filtration experiments.
notable_capabilities: linear pressure-velocity law Q = -k*A*dP/(mu*L) for flow through porous media
first quantitative permeability concept
foundational for paper microfluidics flow modeling
notes: 170-year-old anchor for paper microfluidics and porous-media on-chip flow.
prior_art_notes: Discloses Darcy's law: flux through a porous medium is proportional to the pressure gradient divided by viscosity, with a material-dependent permeability constant. Load-bearing for all paper microfluidic modeling (Whitesides uPADs, lateral flow assays, blood-separation paper devices), sintered-frit and porous-membrane flow control on chip, packed-bed micro-reactors and on-chip chromatography columns. Anticipates patent claims reciting 'pressure-driven flow through porous medium' or 'flow rate proportional to applied pressure through permeable substrate' - Darcy 1856 published the equation 170 years before any microfluidic patent. Particularly invalidates over-broad paper microfluidic claims that fail to disclose specific non-obvious geometries.
sources: Darcy, Les Fontaines Publiques de la Ville de Dijon (1856)
Brown 'Henry Darcy and the making of a law' Water Resour. Res. 38(7), 11 (2002)

canonical_name: Helmholtz 1858 — On integrals of the hydrodynamic equations corresponding to vortex motion
creator: Hermann von Helmholtz
disclosure_citation: H. Helmholtz, 'Über Integrale der hydrodynamischen Gleichungen, welche den Wirbelbewegungen entsprechen', J. Reine Angew. Math. (Crelle) 55, 25-55 (1858)
prior_art_notes: Foundational paper on vortex dynamics; establishes Helmholtz's vortex theorems. For microfluidics, foundational to: chaotic-advection mixers, secondary-flow effects in curved channels (Dean vortices), inertial microfluidics (Di Carlo), and any device exploiting vorticity for particle focusing or mixing. Anticipates: any patent claim that recites controlled vortex generation as its operating principle for mixing or focusing in micro-channels — the underlying vortex theorems are 168 years old.
sources: Crelle J. Reine Angew. Math. vol 55 (1858)

canonical_name: Quincke 1859 - Capillary-rise observations on solid-liquid interfaces
creator: Georg Hermann Quincke
disclosure_citation: Quincke, G. (1859). 'Ueber die Capillaritats-Erscheinungen.' Ann. Phys. Chem. 105: 1-48.
notable_capabilities: systematic measurement of capillary rise heights across solid-liquid pairings
experimental anchor for the contact-angle-controlled meniscus model of Young-Laplace
early quantitative wetting-line dynamics on solid surfaces
notes: Quincke is the 19th-century experimental counterpart to Lucas-Washburn theory; cited as the experimental anchor for paper microfluidic theory.
prior_art_notes: Discloses a systematic experimental program measuring capillary rise heights and meniscus shapes against a range of solid surfaces and liquids, predating Lucas 1918 and Washburn 1921 by six decades. Anticipates paper microfluidic disclosures that recite 'wicking driven by surface tension into porous substrate', 'differential capillary rise rates by surface chemistry', or 'characterization of substrate via observed rise height' - Quincke's 1859 paper documents the experimental basis underlying all such claims. Provides a 19th-century load-bearing anchor for paper microfluidics that complements the Lucas-Washburn dynamic equation already in the corpus.
sources: Quincke wetting bibliography in Bonn et al. RMP 81 (2009)

canonical_name: Wilhelmy 1863 — Plate Method for Surface Tension
creator: Ludwig Wilhelmy
disclosure_citation: Wilhelmy, L. (1863). 'Ueber die Abhaengigkeit der Capillaritaets-Constanten des Alkohols von Substanz und Gestalt des benetzten festen Koerpers.' Annalen der Physik 195(6): 177-217. doi:10.1002/andp.18631950602
notable_capabilities: measurement of surface tension by force on a partially submerged thin plate
established that surface tension is independent of plate material when plate is fully wetted
still the standard tensiometry method 160 years later
prior_art_notes: Discloses surface-tension measurement by force on a vertical plate at the air-liquid interface. Anchors all on-chip surface-tension sensing and contact-angle metrology approaches that derive from interfacial force balance. Anticipates patents claiming 'in-line surface tension measurement' or 'inline interfacial tension probe' to the extent they recite force-on-plate or force-on-fiber geometries.

canonical_name: Tate 1864 — Drop Weight Law (Tate's Law)
creator: Thomas Tate
disclosure_citation: Tate, T. (1864). 'On the magnitude of a drop of liquid formed under different circumstances.' Philosophical Magazine Series 4, 27(181): 176-180.
notable_capabilities: W = 2 pi r gamma: drop weight at detachment from a tube of radius r equals circumference times surface tension
first quantitative theory of pendant-drop formation
underpins all dripping-mode droplet generators
prior_art_notes: Discloses the quantitative relation between droplet detachment volume, orifice radius, and interfacial tension. Anticipates: (a) volumetric metering by drop count (the foundation of stalagmometric dispensing — and by extension every fixed-volume-per-drop dispenser claim); (b) droplet-on-demand sizing in inkjet and microfluidic dispensers when operated below the jetting threshold; (c) calibration of drop volume by surface tension and orifice geometry. Any patent that claims 'fixed-volume droplet dispensing by gravity-detached drops from a known-radius orifice' is anticipated by Tate 1864.

canonical_name: Marangoni 1865 — On the expansion of a droplet of liquid floating on the surface of another liquid (surface-tension-driven flow)
creator: Carlo Giuseppe Matteo Marangoni
disclosure_citation: C. Marangoni, 'Sull'espansione delle goccie d'un liquido galleggianti sulla superfície di altro liquido', Tipografia dei Fratelli Fusi, Pavia (1865); subsequent treatment Nuovo Cim. ser. 2, vol 5/6 (1871)
prior_art_notes: First mathematical and experimental treatment of flows induced by surface-tension gradients (Marangoni effect / Marangoni convection). Foundational for: thermocapillary microfluidic actuation, surfactant-driven droplet motion, evaporation-driven assembly (coffee ring, tear-drop printing), and any droplet-microfluidic process where surfactants modulate interfacial flow. Anticipates: claims to 'thermocapillary microfluidic pump', 'surfactant-driven droplet steering', or 'Marangoni-driven micromixing' as their operating principle — physics is 161 years old.

canonical_name: Marangoni convection (thermocapillary and solutocapillary forms)
creator: Carlo Marangoni (1865); Scriven & Sternling (1960)
disclosure_citation: Extension of: Marangoni, C. (1865). 'Sull espansione delle goccie d un liquido galleggianti sulla superficie di altro liquido.' Pavia. Modern Marangoni convection: Scriven, L. E., Sternling, C. V. (1960). 'The Marangoni effects.' Nature 187: 186-188.
notable_capabilities: surface-tension-gradient-driven convection (thermal: thermocapillary; solutal: solutocapillary)
drives flows tangential to a free surface
load-bearing for evaporation-driven microfluidic flows and thermocapillary pumps
notes: Convective form of the Marangoni effect - anchor for thermocapillary and solutocapillary microfluidics.
prior_art_notes: Companion entry to marangoni-1865-surface-tension-flow (already in corpus), focused on convective form: Marangoni convection. Anticipates thermocapillary-pump microfluidic patents, solutocapillary mixing claims in droplet-on-chip devices, evaporation-driven coffee-ring patterning on chip, Marangoni-driven droplet motion on hydrophilic gradient surfaces, and on-chip droplet self-propulsion patents. Any patent reciting surface-tension-gradient-driven flow in a microfluidic device is anticipated as to the underlying physics.

canonical_name: Maxwell 1867 — On the dynamical theory of gases (kinetic theory of viscosity)
creator: James Clerk Maxwell
disclosure_citation: J.C. Maxwell, 'On the dynamical theory of gases', Phil. Trans. Roy. Soc. London 157, 49-88 (1867)
prior_art_notes: Derivation of gas viscosity from kinetic theory; predicts viscosity is independent of pressure and proportional to sqrt(T). Foundational for: gas-flow microfluidics (gas chromatography on chip, micro gas sensors), Knudsen-number scaling at low pressure, and slip-flow corrections. Anticipates: claims that microscale gas-flow devices exhibit 'unexpected' viscosity behavior as novel — the kinetic-theory framework is 159 years old. Also load-bearing for any breath-analysis lab-on-chip claiming gas-phase transport effects.
sources: Phil. Trans. Roy. Soc. London vol 157 (1867)

canonical_name: Kelvin 1871 — Hydrokinetic solutions and observations (capillary waves and surface tension)
creator: William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin
disclosure_citation: W. Thomson (Lord Kelvin), 'Hydrokinetic solutions and observations', Phil. Mag. ser. 4 vol 42, 362-377 (1871)
prior_art_notes: Kelvin's analysis of capillary-gravity waves on liquid surfaces; establishes the dispersion relation for surface waves under combined surface-tension and gravity. Foundational for: any acoustofluidic device exploiting Faraday waves on a liquid film, capillary-wave-based atomization, or surface-acoustic-wave (SAW) liquid manipulation where capillary waves on the droplet surface participate. Anticipates: capillary-wave atomizer claims and surface-wave-driven micro-mixing claims — the dispersion relation is 155 years old.

canonical_name: Plateau 1873 — Statique expérimentale et théorique des liquides soumis aux seules forces moléculaires
creator: Joseph Antoine Ferdinand Plateau
disclosure_citation: J.A.F. Plateau, 'Statique expérimentale et théorique des liquides soumis aux seules forces moléculaires', Gauthier-Villars, Paris (2 vol., 1873)
prior_art_notes: Foundational treatise on capillarity, soap films, minimal surfaces, and droplet/jet stability. Establishes Plateau's laws (geometry of soap-film junctions and Plateau borders) and the Plateau-Rayleigh instability criterion for jets. Foundational for: any droplet-microfluidic process exploiting jet break-up (flow-focusing, T-junction, co-flow), interfacial geometry (Plateau borders in foams), and minimal-surface microfabrication. Anticipates: claims to droplet generators that recite jet-break-up as their operating principle; the criterion is 153 years old.

canonical_name: Rayleigh 1879 — On the instability of jets (Plateau-Rayleigh instability)
creator: John William Strutt, 3rd Baron Rayleigh
disclosure_citation: Lord Rayleigh, 'On the instability of jets', Proc. London Math. Soc. s1-10, 4-13 (1879); doi:10.1112/plms/s1-10.1.4
prior_art_notes: Quantitative linear-stability analysis showing that a cylindrical liquid jet is unstable to perturbations of wavelength greater than its circumference (most-unstable wavelength ≈ 9.02 r), leading to break-up into droplets. Anticipates: every droplet-microfluidic generator (T-junction, flow-focusing, co-flow), every continuous-inkjet printhead, every drop-on-demand piezo printhead, every microfluidic emulsion generator. The criterion is the operating physics of these devices and is 147 years old. Particularly load-bearing for inkjet/drop-generator patents claiming 'a method of producing droplets of controlled size by perturbing a liquid jet'.

canonical_name: Helmholtz 1879 — Electrical Double Layer and Electroosmosis
creator: Hermann von Helmholtz
disclosure_citation: Helmholtz, H. v. (1879). 'Studien ueber elektrische Grenzschichten.' Annalen der Physik und Chemie 243(7): 337-382. doi:10.1002/andp.18792430702
notable_capabilities: first quantitative theory of the electrical double layer at solid-liquid interfaces
explanation of electroosmosis, electrophoresis, streaming potential as related electrokinetic phenomena
concept of compact (Helmholtz) layer of counter-ions adjacent to charged surface
prior_art_notes: Discloses the electrical-double-layer concept that anchors all electrokinetic microfluidic phenomena: electroosmotic flow, electrophoresis, streaming potential, sedimentation potential, dielectrophoresis (in part). Predates Smoluchowski 1903's quantitative slip-velocity by 24 years. Anticipates broad patent claims to 'voltage-controlled flow', 'surface-charge-modulated transport', or 'streaming-potential sensing on a chip' insofar as they recite the underlying double-layer physics.

canonical_name: Plateau-Rayleigh instability (combined droplet-formation theory)
creator: Joseph Plateau (1873); Lord Rayleigh (1879)
disclosure_citation: Combined: Plateau, J. (1873). 'Statique experimentale et theorique des liquides soumis aux seules forces moleculaires.' Gauthier-Villars, Paris. AND Rayleigh, Lord (1879). 'On the instability of jets.' Proc. London Math. Soc. 10: 4-13.
notable_capabilities: combined classical theory of liquid-jet breakup into droplets
wavelength of fastest-growing instability (~9.02*R for inviscid jets)
load-bearing for ALL droplet-generation microfluidics
notes: Combined-anchor entry: Plateau-Rayleigh as the universal name for the droplet-jet-breakup instability.
prior_art_notes: Combined entry for the Plateau-Rayleigh instability, the foundational classical theory underlying every microfluidic droplet generator (T-junction, flow-focusing, co-flow, step-emulsification). Plateau 1873 (experimental anchor on existence of the instability) plus Rayleigh 1879 (analytical derivation of the most-unstable wavelength) together publish 'a liquid jet breaks into droplets at a wavelength determined by surface tension and inertia' in the public literature 150 years before any droplet-microfluidic patent. Anticipates any patent claim reciting droplet-size selection from a continuous jet - Plateau-Rayleigh predicts the wavelength and growth rate. Combined entry exists so the dual-anchor citation is searchable as a single prior-art reference.

canonical_name: An experimental investigation of the circumstances which determine flow regime
creator: Osborne Reynolds (Manchester)
disclosure_citation: Reynolds, O. An experimental investigation of the circumstances which determine whether the motion of water shall be direct or sinuous, and of the law of resistance in parallel channels. Philos. Trans. R. Soc. London 1883, 174, 935–982. DOI: 10.1098/rstl.1883.0029
notes: Predates microfluidics by a century; included as the foundational fluid-mechanics anchor that every microfluidic paper implicitly cites.
prior_art_notes: The foundational paper of fluid mechanics relevant to microfluidics: defines the Reynolds number Re = ρUL/µ and demonstrates that pipe flow transitions from laminar to turbulent at Re ≈ 2000. Microfluidic flow operates almost universally at Re < 1, deep in the laminar regime, which is why diffusive mixing dominates and why most of microfluidics' counterintuitive behavior follows. Cited as the de facto first reference in any rigorous microfluidic theory paper. Doctrinally relevant for invalidity contention against any patent claiming 'novel laminar-flow microfluidic separation' as a category — the laminar regime itself is 140 years old.

canonical_name: Reynolds Number Re = rho U L / mu
creator: Osborne Reynolds (group); Arnold Sommerfeld (naming)
disclosure_citation: Reynolds, O. (1883). 'An experimental investigation of the circumstances which determine whether the motion of water shall be direct or sinuous.' Phil. Trans. R. Soc. 174: 935-982. doi:10.1098/rstl.1883.0029. Group named by Sommerfeld in 1908.
notable_capabilities: Re = rho U L / mu — ratio of inertial to viscous forces
Re < ~2000 -> laminar pipe flow; Re > ~4000 -> turbulent (rough cutoffs)
the universal scaling parameter dividing low-Re (microfluidic) from high-Re (macro) regimes
notes: Separate dimensionless-group entry; complements the Reynolds 1883 paper anchor.
prior_art_notes: Reynolds number is the single most invoked dimensionless group in microfluidic literature; nearly every microfluidic chip operates at Re << 1 by design (channel size ~10 to 100 microns; velocity ~mm/s; water viscosity). Anchors: (a) all 'laminar flow chip' patents (Yager H-filter, parallel-stream extraction); (b) all 'inertial microfluidics' (Di Carlo 2007) patents that explicitly key on Re ~ 1-100; (c) the Purcell scallop theorem foundation (Purcell 1977); (d) Reynolds-controlled droplet generation regime. Codified by Sommerfeld in 1908. Together with Reynolds 1883 (the experimental paper) this anchors all dimensionless-group reasoning that microfluidic IP relies on.
sources: Sommerfeld, A. (1908) Atti del IV Congresso Internazionale dei Matematici, Roma, vol. III, 116-124

canonical_name: Reynolds 1886/1903 — Reynolds equation of lubrication theory (thin-film flow)
creator: Osborne Reynolds
disclosure_citation: O. Reynolds, 'On the theory of lubrication and its application to Mr. Beauchamp Tower's experiments', Phil. Trans. Roy. Soc. London 177, 157-234 (1886); reprinted in O. Reynolds, Scientific Papers vol 2 (Cambridge Univ. Press, 1901)
prior_art_notes: Foundational derivation of the Reynolds lubrication equation governing thin-film flow between nearly parallel surfaces. Foundational for: Hele-Shaw cell microfluidics, valve-membrane closure dynamics, squeeze-film damping in MEMS, and any microfluidic process where the flow occurs in a gap of small aspect ratio. Anticipates: claims to 'thin-film microfluidic device' or 'membrane valve with controlled closure dynamics' whose operating physics is the Reynolds equation — derivation is 140 years old.
sources: Phil. Trans. Roy. Soc. London vol 177 (1886)

canonical_name: Bond / Eoetvoes Number Bo = rho g L^2 / gamma
creator: Lorand Eoetvoes (1886); Wilfrid Noel Bond (1928 dimensionless form)
disclosure_citation: Eoetvoes, R. (1886). 'Ueber den Zusammenhang der Oberflaechenspannung der Fluessigkeiten mit ihrem Molekularvolumen.' Annalen der Physik 263(3): 448-459. doi:10.1002/andp.18862630309. Bond, W. N. (1928). Proc. Phys. Soc. 41, 1.
notable_capabilities: Bo = rho g L^2 / gamma — ratio of gravity to surface tension
Bo << 1 (small chips, water): gravity negligible; surface tension dominates
predicts capillary length L_c = sqrt(gamma / rho g) ~ 2.7 mm for water
prior_art_notes: Bond number explains why microfluidics works at all: at L ~ 100 microns, Bo ~ 10^-3 for water, so gravity is irrelevant and surface tension dominates. This is THE physical foundation for the microfluidic regime; anchors every patent claim that recites 'gravity-independent operation', 'orientation-independent chip', or 'surface-tension-driven liquid handling'. Eoetvoes 1886 (the equivalent group) predates the entire modern microfluidic field by more than a century.
sources: Bond, W. N. Proc. Phys. Soc. 41, 1 (1928)

canonical_name: Couette 1890 — Concentric Cylinder Viscometer and Couette Flow
creator: Maurice Couette
disclosure_citation: Couette, M. (1890). 'Etudes sur le frottement des liquides.' Annales de Chimie et de Physique Series 6, 21: 433-510; abridged Couette, M. (1890). J. Phys. Theor. Appl. 9(1): 414-417. doi:10.1051/jphystap:018900090041401
notable_capabilities: shear-driven flow between two surfaces in relative motion (planar Couette) or rotating concentric cylinders (Taylor-Couette)
first quantitative shear viscometer
linear velocity profile under steady shear
prior_art_notes: Discloses the canonical shear-driven flow geometry. Anchors: (a) all shear-controlled microfluidic devices including blood-cell deformability assays; (b) on-chip rheometry; (c) shear-stress-controlled cell-culture chips (vascular shear); (d) Taylor-Couette mixing reactors at small scale; (e) any flow chamber that imposes a controlled shear via a moving boundary. Anticipates patent claims reciting 'controlled shear stress on cells by parallel-plate flow chamber', 'rotating-disc on-chip shear', or 'concentric-cylinder cell-stressing geometry' insofar as the shear-flow geometry is the only novel feature.

canonical_name: Hele-Shaw 1898 — The Flow of Water (Hele-Shaw Cell)
creator: Henry Selby Hele-Shaw
disclosure_citation: Hele-Shaw, H. S. (1898). 'The flow of water.' Nature 58(1489): 34-36. doi:10.1038/058034a0; followed by Hele-Shaw, H. S. (1898). 'Investigation of the nature of surface resistance of water and of stream-line motion under certain experimental conditions.' Trans. Inst. Naval Arch. 40: 21-46.
notable_capabilities: thin-gap geometry (two parallel plates separated by small gap h) yields depth-averaged flow obeying potential-flow equations
visualization of streamline patterns around obstacles
demonstrated equivalence between Hele-Shaw flow and 2D potential flow / Darcy flow
notes: Single most underappreciated 19th-century anchor for microfluidic geometry; the entire 'shallow rectangular channel' class is Hele-Shaw flow.
prior_art_notes: Discloses the canonical thin-slit geometry now ubiquitous in microfluidic chip design. Every PDMS or glass slit-channel device that is wider than it is tall operates in the Hele-Shaw regime, and Hele-Shaw 1898 is the explicit prior art for: (a) all 'flat-channel microfluidic chip' geometries that claim depth-averaged flow behavior; (b) viscous fingering experiments (Saffman-Taylor 1958); (c) Darcy-equivalent porous-medium analog devices used for petroleum-engineering and groundwater education chips; (d) all chips that rely on the equivalence between Hele-Shaw cell flow and 2D Laplace equation for streamline visualization. Anticipates patent claims that recite 'a flat microchannel of width >> depth' or 'depth-averaged 2D flow chip', stripping such broad geometric claims of novelty over Hele-Shaw 1898.

canonical_name: Forchheimer 1901 - Wasserbewegung durch Boden (high-velocity porous flow)
creator: Philipp Forchheimer
disclosure_citation: Forchheimer, P. (1901). 'Wasserbewegung durch Boden.' Zeitschrift des Vereines Deutscher Ingenieure 45: 1782-1788.
notable_capabilities: nonlinear pressure-velocity law -dP/dx = (mu/k)*u + beta*rho*u^2 for high-Re porous flow
quadratic inertial correction to Darcy law
applicable to packed-bed microreactors at moderate Re
notes: Forchheimer extends Darcy into higher-Re regime relevant to packed-bed microreactors.
prior_art_notes: Discloses the Forchheimer equation: a quadratic-in-velocity correction to Darcy's law valid at higher Reynolds numbers in porous media. Anticipates patent claims involving packed-bed microreactors operating at non-negligible Re, on-chip packed columns for chromatography or solid-phase extraction at high throughput, particle-bed filters for whole-blood handling - any disclosure claiming a flow-rate-vs-pressure relationship beyond pure Darcy is anticipated by Forchheimer 1901.

canonical_name: Smoluchowski 1903 — Electroosmotic Velocity Equation
creator: Marian Smoluchowski
disclosure_citation: Smoluchowski, M. v. (1903). 'Contribution a la theorie de l'endosmose electrique et de quelques phenomenes correlatifs.' Bulletin International de l'Academie des Sciences de Cracovie 8: 182-200.
notable_capabilities: electroosmotic slip velocity u_eo = -(epsilon zeta / mu) E
extension of Helmholtz 1879 EOF observations to a quantitative electrokinetic theory
predicts plug-flow velocity profile for thin double layer (Debye length << channel)
notes: Single most load-bearing classical anchor for electrokinetic microfluidics.
prior_art_notes: Discloses the Helmholtz-Smoluchowski equation, which is THE governing relation for all electroosmotic-flow microfluidic devices. Every capillary electrophoresis chip, every electrokinetic pump, every electroosmotic micromixer, every iontophoresis-on-chip drug-delivery system inherits its quantitative behavior from Smoluchowski 1903. Anticipates: (a) all patent claims to 'electrokinetically driven liquid transport' that fail to recite a specific non-obvious geometry; (b) zeta-potential-controlled flow rate claims; (c) field-strength-modulated EOF pumping claims; (d) the entire class of EOF capillary pumps used in micro total analysis systems (Manz 1990 successor patents). The plug-flow EOF profile (advantageous for electrophoresis because it minimizes Taylor-Aris dispersion) was disclosed in 1903.

aliases: Ueber Fluessigkeitsbewegung bei sehr kleiner Reibung
canonical_name: Prandtl 1904 — Boundary Layer Theory
creator: Ludwig Prandtl
disclosure_citation: Prandtl, L. (1904). 'Ueber Fluessigkeitsbewegung bei sehr kleiner Reibung.' Verhandlungen des dritten internationalen Mathematiker-Kongresses, Heidelberg, 8-13 August 1904: 484-491. Teubner, Leipzig (1905).
notable_capabilities: division of high-Reynolds flow into thin viscous boundary layer near walls and inviscid outer flow
boundary layer equations as parabolic simplification of Navier-Stokes
explanation of separation, drag, and the no-slip condition's far-field consequences
prior_art_notes: While microfluidic flows are typically low-Reynolds (laminar throughout), Prandtl's boundary-layer concept is foundational for: (a) entry-length analysis in microchannels (Schlichting boundary-layer growth in developing flow); (b) high-Re inertial microfluidics (Di Carlo 2007 and descendants — particles migrate based on competing inertial lift and shear forces, both of which derive from boundary-layer arguments); (c) jet-impingement microchannel cooling (Tuckerman-Pease descendants). Anticipates: any patent claiming 'particle focusing by boundary-layer-mediated inertial lift' to the extent it recites boundary-layer physics generally rather than a specific non-obvious channel geometry.
sources: Verh. III. Internat. Math.-Kongress, Heidelberg (1904) pp. 484-491

canonical_name: Sutherland 1905 — Independent Derivation of Brownian Motion / Stokes-Einstein
creator: William Sutherland
disclosure_citation: Sutherland, W. (1905). 'A dynamical theory of diffusion for non-electrolytes and the molecular mass of albumin.' Philosophical Magazine Series 6, 9(54): 781-785. doi:10.1080/14786440509463331
notable_capabilities: independent contemporaneous derivation of D = kT / (6 pi mu r) two months before Einstein
applied to determination of protein molecular mass from diffusion data
demonstrated relevance to biological macromolecules from the start
prior_art_notes: Sutherland published the equation now usually called Stokes-Einstein two months before Einstein, in the context of protein-molecular-mass determination. Provides an even earlier prior-art anchor than Einstein 1905 for any patent claim resting on Stokes-Einstein diffusion. Particularly important for invalidating patents that claim the application of D = kT / (6 pi mu r) to protein/biomolecule sizing.

canonical_name: Einstein 1905 — Brownian Motion and Stokes-Einstein Diffusion
creator: Albert Einstein
disclosure_citation: Einstein, A. (1905). 'Ueber die von der molekularkinetischen Theorie der Waerme geforderte Bewegung von in ruhenden Fluessigkeiten suspendierten Teilchen.' Annalen der Physik 322(8): 549-560. doi:10.1002/andp.19053220806
notable_capabilities: mean-square displacement <x^2> = 2 D t for Brownian particles
Stokes-Einstein diffusion coefficient D = kT / (6 pi mu r)
predicts particle size from diffusion measurement
prior_art_notes: The Stokes-Einstein equation governs every diffusion-limited microfluidic process: H-filter separations (Brody and Yager 1997), diffusion mixers, Taylor-Aris dispersion (combined with Aris 1956), nanoparticle sizing by FCS or NTA, and the diffusion-controlled inlet/outlet of every reagent-zone in paper microfluidics. Anticipates patent claims that recite 'separation by diffusion coefficient difference' or 'particle sizing by Brownian motion tracking' insofar as they rest on the Stokes-Einstein relation. Together with Sutherland 1905 (independent derivation) this anchors over 120 years of diffusion-based microfluidic prior art.

canonical_name: Langevin 1908 — Stochastic Equation for Brownian Motion
creator: Paul Langevin
disclosure_citation: Langevin, P. (1908). 'Sur la theorie du mouvement brownien.' Comptes Rendus de l'Academie des Sciences (Paris) 146: 530-533.
notable_capabilities: m dv/dt = -gamma v + F(t) stochastic equation of motion
introduces fluctuation force F(t) with delta-correlated statistics
alternative derivation of Stokes-Einstein result via stochastic dynamics
prior_art_notes: Langevin's stochastic differential equation underpins all numerical simulation of Brownian dynamics in microfluidic systems (single-particle tracking, electrokinetic transport at low ionic concentration, optical-tweezers calibration on chip). Anticipates patent claims to 'simulation-driven control of microfluidic particle trajectories' that rest on Langevin dynamics, particularly in the context of feedback-controlled trapping.

canonical_name: Knudsen 1909 — The molecular current of gases through tubes (Knudsen number)
creator: Martin Knudsen
disclosure_citation: M. Knudsen, 'Die Gesetze der Molekularströmung und der inneren Reibungsströmung der Gase durch Röhren', Annalen der Physik 333(1), 75-130 (1909)
prior_art_notes: Foundational treatment of gas flow in narrow tubes when mean free path is comparable to channel width; introduces what becomes known as the Knudsen number Kn=λ/L and the slip/transition/free-molecular flow regimes. Anticipates: any nanofluidic or vacuum-microfluidic patent that claims operation in the slip or transition regime as novel — the regime classification is 117 years old. Particularly load-bearing for: Knudsen-pump devices, MEMS gas sensors, and nanopore gas-transport devices.

canonical_name: Knudsen Number Kn = lambda / L
creator: Martin Knudsen
disclosure_citation: Knudsen, M. (1909). 'Die Gesetze der Molekularstroemung und der inneren Reibungsstroemung der Gase durch Roehren.' Annalen der Physik 333(1): 75-130. doi:10.1002/andp.19093330106. Group structure implicit; standardized in 20th-century rarefied-gas literature.
notable_capabilities: Kn = lambda / L — ratio of mean free path to characteristic length
Kn < 0.001: continuum; 0.001 < Kn < 0.1: slip flow; 0.1 < Kn < 10: transition; Kn > 10: free molecular
anchors all gas-phase microfluidic and nanofluidic transport
notes: Separate dimensionless-group entry; complements knudsen-1909-gas-flow-narrow-tubes paper anchor.
prior_art_notes: Knudsen number is the controlling regime parameter for gas-phase microfluidics, vacuum microfluidics, and nanofluidic gas separations. At ~100 nm channels with air at STP, Kn ~ 1 and continuum equations break down. Anticipates: (a) all gas-microfluidic claims that recite slip-flow boundary conditions; (b) Knudsen pumps (thermal transpiration); (c) nanopore gas separation patents; (d) Pirani gauge on-chip claims. Together with Knudsen 1909 (the source paper) anchors all rarefied-gas microfluidic prior art.

canonical_name: Gouy 1910 — Diffuse Double Layer Theory
creator: Louis Georges Gouy
disclosure_citation: Gouy, G. (1910). 'Sur la constitution de la charge electrique a la surface d'un electrolyte.' J. Phys. Theor. Appl. 9(1): 457-468. doi:10.1051/jphystap:019100090045700
notable_capabilities: replaces Helmholtz's compact double layer with a diffuse Boltzmann-distributed counterion cloud
predicts exponential potential decay from charged surface
introduces concept of effective screening length (precursor to Debye length)
prior_art_notes: Discloses the diffuse double layer that governs all nanofluidic ion-transport behavior including the regime where channel dimension is comparable to the Debye length (the 'overlapping double layer' regime that anchors nanofluidic ionic-current rectification, ionic transistors, and selective ion sieves). Anticipates broad patent claims to 'ionic selectivity by Debye-length matched channel dimension' or 'rectifying nanofluidic ion transport' insofar as those rest on diffuse-layer physics.

canonical_name: Chapman 1913 — Diffuse Double Layer Extension
creator: David Leonard Chapman
disclosure_citation: Chapman, D. L. (1913). 'A contribution to the theory of electrocapillarity.' Philosophical Magazine Series 6, 25(148): 475-481. doi:10.1080/14786440408634187
notable_capabilities: independent derivation matching Gouy 1910's diffuse double layer
Poisson-Boltzmann analytical solution for planar geometry
completes the Gouy-Chapman theory of electrocapillarity
prior_art_notes: Co-anchors the Gouy-Chapman model of the diffuse double layer underpinning all electrokinetic microfluidics. Together with Gouy 1910, anticipates any patent claim to ionic-current-rectifying nanopores, surface-charge-tuned EOF, or Debye-length-controlled selectivity that fails to recite a non-obvious geometry beyond the underlying physics.

canonical_name: Smoluchowski 1916 — Diffusion-Controlled Coagulation Theory
creator: Marian Smoluchowski
disclosure_citation: Smoluchowski, M. v. (1916). 'Drei Vortraege ueber Diffusion, Brownsche Bewegung und Koagulation von Kolloidteilchen.' Physikalische Zeitschrift 17: 557-571 and 585-599.
notable_capabilities: k_diff = 4 pi (D_A + D_B)(r_A + r_B) diffusion-limited reaction rate
kinetic equations for size-distribution evolution under coagulation
first quantitative theory of diffusion-controlled chemistry
prior_art_notes: Smoluchowski's diffusion-controlled rate constant is the upper bound on every on-chip biochemical reaction rate. Anticipates: (a) immunoassay binding-time predictions in microfluidic devices (the Sqalli-Houssini bound on antibody capture); (b) DNA-target hybridization rates on microfluidic biosensors; (c) particle-aggregation assay timing claims; (d) molecular-beacon and aptamer-binding cartridge claims that rest on diffusion-limited kinetics. Any patent claim to 'rapid diagnosis by surface-capture in a microchannel' is bounded above by Smoluchowski 1916 and cannot claim novelty over the diffusion-limited rate.

canonical_name: Lucas 1918 — Capillary Rise Dynamics
creator: Richard Lucas
disclosure_citation: Lucas, R. (1918). 'Ueber das Zeitgesetz des kapillaren Aufstiegs von Fluessigkeiten.' Kolloid-Zeitschrift 23(1): 15-22. doi:10.1007/BF01461107
notable_capabilities: time-dependent capillary rise law h(t) ~ sqrt(t) for viscous-dominated regime
predates Washburn 1921 by three years
balances capillary pressure against viscous drag (Hagen-Poiseuille)
prior_art_notes: Discloses that the rise height of a wetting liquid in a capillary scales as the square root of time (h proportional to sqrt(gamma r cos(theta) t / mu)). This Lucas equation is the immediate prior art for: (a) all paper microfluidic / lateral-flow assay timing claims that recite a sqrt(t) wicking law; (b) self-priming microfluidic channels with predictable fill time; (c) wicking-pad reagent-storage cartridges. Together with Washburn 1921 (Lucas-Washburn equation) it anchors more than a century of capillary-flow patent prior art. Critically, Lucas 1918 PREDATES Washburn 1921 — examiners frequently cite only Washburn, leaving Lucas as a stronger anchor for invalidating priority claims that key on the 1921 date.

canonical_name: Weber 1919 — Weber Number We = rho U^2 L / gamma
creator: Moritz Weber
disclosure_citation: Weber, M. (1919). 'Die Grundlagen der Aehnlichkeitsmechanik und ihre Verwertung bei Modellversuchen.' Jahrbuch der Schiffbautechnischen Gesellschaft 20: 355-477.
notable_capabilities: We = rho U^2 L / gamma — ratio of inertia to surface tension
controls droplet impact, splashing, jet break-up regimes
complements Capillary number (Ca = We/Re)
prior_art_notes: Weber number governs droplet impact, jet break-up onset, and high-velocity droplet-on-demand inkjet ejection. Anchors: (a) all inkjet drop-formation patents that recite a velocity-controlled droplet size; (b) impingement-mixing on-chip patents; (c) high-throughput droplet generation in jetting regime; (d) splashing-controlled droplet deposition for additive manufacturing. Predates the modern droplet-microfluidics field by 75 years.
sources: Weber, M. Jahrbuch der Schiffbautechnischen Gesellschaft 20, 355 (1919)

canonical_name: Washburn 1921 — The Dynamics of Capillary Flow
creator: Edward W. Washburn
disclosure_citation: Washburn, E. W. (1921). 'The dynamics of capillary flow.' Physical Review 17(3): 273-283. doi:10.1103/PhysRev.17.273
notable_capabilities: x^2 = (gamma r cos(theta) / 2 mu) t penetration law for porous media and capillaries
extension to non-circular cross sections
treatment of inertial regime at early times
prior_art_notes: Discloses the canonical Washburn equation governing capillary-driven liquid penetration into porous media and small-bore tubes. This is THE prior-art anchor for paper-based microfluidics: every commercial lateral-flow assay (pregnancy tests, COVID antigen tests, etc.) operates in the Washburn regime and any patent that claims 'control of assay timing by paper geometry and surface tension' or 'reagent zone metering by Washburn flow' is anticipated. Specifically anticipates: (a) flow-rate control by channel-width modulation in paper devices (Martinez 2007 and descendants); (b) timed reagent release via fluidic-resistance shaping; (c) multi-zone paper devices that rely on predictable wicking front arrival times. Washburn 1921 is uniformly cited by all paper-microfluidic invalidity contentions.

canonical_name: Debye-Hueckel 1923 — Debye Length and Strong Electrolyte Theory
creator: Peter Debye; Erich Hueckel
disclosure_citation: Debye, P., Hueckel, E. (1923). 'Zur Theorie der Elektrolyte. I. Gefrierpunktserniedrigung und verwandte Erscheinungen.' Physikalische Zeitschrift 24: 185-206; II. ibid. 305-325.
notable_capabilities: Debye screening length lambda_D = sqrt(epsilon kT / 2 n_0 z^2 e^2)
linearized Poisson-Boltzmann equation for dilute electrolytes
explanation of activity coefficients in strong electrolytes
prior_art_notes: Defines the Debye length, the single most-cited length scale in nanofluidics. Every claim in nanofluidic patents that recites a 'channel dimension comparable to the Debye length', 'overlapping double-layer regime', or 'ionic selectivity controlled by salt concentration' inherits from Debye-Hueckel 1923. Anticipates broad nanofluidic IP that fails to disclose specific non-obvious geometric features beyond the Debye-length matching.

canonical_name: Stern 1924 — Stern Layer Theory
creator: Otto Stern
disclosure_citation: Stern, O. (1924). 'Zur Theorie der elektrolytischen Doppelschicht.' Zeitschrift fuer Elektrochemie und angewandte physikalische Chemie 30(21-22): 508-516. doi:10.1002/bbpc.192400182
notable_capabilities: combines Helmholtz compact layer with Gouy-Chapman diffuse layer
introduces ion-size limit (Stern adsorption plane)
modern Gouy-Chapman-Stern model used in all electrokinetic device design
prior_art_notes: Completes the modern theory of the electric double layer used in all electrokinetic microfluidic and nanofluidic device design. The zeta potential (the potential at the slip plane just outside the Stern layer) is the parameter every commercial EOF pump, every CE chip, and every electrokinetic micromixer is calibrated against. Anticipates patent claims keyed on 'controlled zeta potential surface coatings', 'adsorbed-ion modulated EOF', or 'Stern-layer engineering' as electrokinetic control schemes.

canonical_name: Kozeny 1927 - Uber kapillare Leitung des Wassers im Boden
creator: Josef Kozeny
disclosure_citation: Kozeny, J. (1927). 'Uber kapillare Leitung des Wassers im Boden.' Sitzungsberichte der Akademie der Wissenschaften in Wien 136: 271-306.
notable_capabilities: geometric model relating permeability to porosity and specific surface area
capillary-bundle conception of porous medium
foundational for the Carman-Kozeny equation
notes: Foundational for Carman-Kozeny composite.
prior_art_notes: Kozeny modeled a porous medium as a bundle of parallel capillaries of equivalent surface area and derived k = phi^3/(c*S^2). Anticipates any microfluidic disclosure that derives permeability from fiber-mat or particle-bed geometry - paper microfluidic flow-time predictions, cell-trap arrays modeled as porous regions, packed-bead microreactor predictions. Load-bearing for any patent claim reciting 'permeability calculated from substrate porosity and specific surface area' or 'flow-rate predicted from geometric porous-medium model'.

canonical_name: Capillary Number Ca = mu U / gamma
creator: tradition (group structure implicit since 19th-century capillary-flow work)
disclosure_citation: Bond, W. N. (1928). 'The use of dimensionless equations.' Proc. Phys. Soc. London 41(1): 1-16; named by Taylor in subsequent capillary-flow literature. Implicit in Tate 1864, Plateau 1873, Rayleigh 1879 work on droplet break-up.
notable_capabilities: Ca = mu U / gamma — ratio of viscous to surface-tension forces
controls droplet break-up regime in T-junction and flow-focusing generators
low Ca -> dripping; high Ca -> jetting
prior_art_notes: Capillary number is the controlling parameter for every droplet generator. The dripping-to-jetting transition, the squeezing-to-shearing transition in T-junctions, and the droplet-size scaling laws in flow-focusing devices are all functions of Ca. Anchors: (a) all droplet-generator patents that recite a flow-rate-to-droplet-size scaling (Anna 2003, Thorsen 2002, Garstecki 2006); (b) co-flow droplet sizing claims; (c) step-emulsification regime maps. Any patent claim that recites operating conditions in terms of viscosity, velocity, and surface tension is anticipated by the capillary-number scaling.
sources: Bond, W. N. Proc. Phys. Soc. 41, 1 (1928)
Taylor, G. I. on droplet deformation in shear (1934)

canonical_name: Schmidt Number Sc = nu / D
creator: Ernst Schmidt
disclosure_citation: Schmidt, E. (1929). 'Foeppls Festschrift,' Springer-Verlag, Berlin, p. 179. Group structure standardized in subsequent transport literature.
notable_capabilities: Sc = nu / D — ratio of momentum to mass diffusivity
Sc ~ 1 for gases; Sc ~ 1000 for small molecules in water; Sc ~ 10^6 for proteins in water
Pe = Re * Sc links velocity-domain Re to mass-transport
prior_art_notes: Schmidt number is the mass-transport analog of Prandtl number and links Reynolds and Peclet numbers. In aqueous microfluidics, the very large Sc means that mass mixing is much harder than momentum diffusion — this is the physical reason mixing is the central design problem in microfluidic chemistry. Anchors: (a) all 'mixing-enhancement' patents that recite an enhanced effective Schmidt number; (b) lamination-mixer scaling-law claims; (c) proteomic on-chip extraction efficiency arguments.
sources: Schmidt, E. in Foeppls Festschrift (Springer 1929) p. 179

canonical_name: Onsager 1931 — Reciprocal Relations
creator: Lars Onsager
disclosure_citation: Onsager, L. (1931). 'Reciprocal relations in irreversible processes. I.' Physical Review 37(4): 405-426. doi:10.1103/PhysRev.37.405; II. ibid. 38, 2265-2279 (1931).
notable_capabilities: reciprocity between coupled fluxes in linear-response thermodynamics: L_ij = L_ji
predicts that electroosmosis and streaming potential coefficients are equal
predicts that thermodiffusion (Soret) and Dufour coefficients are linked
prior_art_notes: Onsager's reciprocal relations directly link electroosmosis to streaming potential, and electrophoresis to sedimentation potential. This means any microfluidic device that exploits one electrokinetic effect (e.g., streaming-potential energy harvesting from pressure-driven flow in a charged microchannel) is anticipated by Onsager 1931 in combination with the corresponding inverse-effect prior art. Anticipates: (a) streaming-potential micropumps and energy-harvesting chips; (b) thermo-osmotic pumps; (c) any 'cross-coupled transport' microfluidic claim that rests on Onsager-reciprocal physics. Onsager won the 1968 Nobel Prize in Chemistry largely for this 1931 paper.

canonical_name: King 1934 - On the acoustic radiation pressure on spheres
creator: Louis V. King
disclosure_citation: King, L. V. (1934). 'On the acoustic radiation pressure on spheres.' Proc. R. Soc. A 147(861): 212-240. doi:10.1098/rspa.1934.0215
notable_capabilities: first complete theoretical treatment of acoustic radiation pressure on rigid spheres in plane waves
scaling laws relating radiation force to sphere radius, wavelength, density contrast
foundational for acoustofluidic particle handling
notes: Foundational acoustic-radiation-pressure paper - 90-year-old anchor for ALL acoustofluidics.
prior_art_notes: King 1934 derives the canonical acoustic-radiation-force expression on rigid spheres in standing or traveling plane waves. Load-bearing relation underlying every acoustofluidic separation, trap, and focuser: bulk acoustic-wave (BAW) chambers, surface-acoustic-wave (SAW) particle manipulators, acoustic-streaming traps. Anticipates patent claims reciting 'acoustic radiation force used to focus particles by size or density' or 'standing-wave node trapping of cells/beads' - the underlying physics has been in public literature since 1934.

canonical_name: Tomotika 1935 - On the instability of a cylindrical thread of a viscous liquid surrounded by another viscous fluid
creator: Susumu Tomotika
disclosure_citation: Tomotika, S. (1935). 'On the instability of a cylindrical thread of a viscous liquid surrounded by another viscous fluid.' Proc. R. Soc. A 150(870): 322-337. doi:10.1098/rspa.1935.0104
notable_capabilities: extension of Plateau-Rayleigh instability to a viscous cylindrical thread in a viscous outer phase
viscosity-ratio-dependent breakup wavelength and growth rate
load-bearing for droplet-generation theory in microfluidic emulsifiers
notes: Anchor for viscous-jet droplet breakup theory in microfluidic flow-focusing devices.
prior_art_notes: Tomotika 1935 extends the Plateau-Rayleigh instability (1873/1879, both in corpus) to viscous cylindrical threads surrounded by a second viscous fluid - the canonical flow-focusing/co-flow droplet-generator geometry at microscale. Anticipates any patent claim reciting droplet-size selection by viscosity ratio, viscous-jet breakup in microfluidic flow-focusing channels, or wavelength-keyed droplet diameter prediction - all reduce to Tomotika scaling.

canonical_name: Damkoehler Numbers Da_I, Da_II
creator: Gerhard Damkoehler
disclosure_citation: Damkoehler, G. (1936). 'Einfluesse der Stroemung, Diffusion und des Waermeueberganges auf die Leistung von Reaktionsoefen.' Z. Elektrochem. 42(12): 846-862.
notable_capabilities: Da_I = k tau (reaction rate * residence time) — reaction vs flow
Da_II = k L^2 / D (reaction vs diffusion)
controls conversion in continuous-flow microreactors
prior_art_notes: Damkoehler numbers govern every continuous-flow microreactor: Da_I sets conversion as a function of flow rate; Da_II sets whether the reactor is reaction- or diffusion-limited. Anchors: (a) all flow-chemistry microreactor patents reciting residence-time control; (b) on-chip enzymatic-assay timing claims; (c) on-chip PCR amplification residence-time engineering; (d) heterogeneous catalysis microreactors. Any patent claim that recites 'tunable conversion via residence-time modulation' is anticipated by Damkoehler scaling.

canonical_name: Carman 1937 - Permeability of saturated sands, soils and clays (Carman-Kozeny equation)
creator: Philip C. Carman
disclosure_citation: Carman, P. C. (1937). 'Fluid flow through granular beds.' Trans. IChemE 15: 150-166. Companion: Carman, P. C. (1939). J. Agric. Sci. 29: 263.
notable_capabilities: Carman-Kozeny equation k = phi^3/(K_CK * (1-phi)^2 * S_v^2) for permeability of granular media
empirically calibrated for packed beds of spherical particles
load-bearing for packed-bed bioreactors and chromatography columns on chip
notes: Permeability anchor for packed-bed on-chip columns.
prior_art_notes: Combines Kozeny's geometric capillary-bundle model with Carman's empirical permeability data into the Carman-Kozeny equation, the standard relation for permeability of granular and fibrous porous media. Anticipates microfluidic disclosures claiming packed-bead immunoassay columns with predicted flow rates, on-chip solid-phase extraction columns sized to a target pressure drop, cell-trap arrays modeled as porous media. Any patent claim that derives an on-chip permeability or pressure-drop from bead-diameter and packing fraction is anticipated by Carman-Kozeny.

canonical_name: Derjaguin & Landau 1941 - Theory of the stability of strongly charged lyophobic sols
creator: Boris V. Derjaguin; Lev D. Landau
disclosure_citation: Derjaguin, B., Landau, L. (1941). 'Theory of the stability of strongly charged lyophobic sols and of the adhesion of strongly charged particles in solutions of electrolytes.' Acta Physicochim. USSR 14: 633-662.
notable_capabilities: independent derivation of the DLVO criterion for colloid stability
electric-double-layer + van der Waals interaction analysis
one half of the DLVO acronym
notes: Soviet-side anchor for DLVO; pairs with Verwey-Overbeek 1948.
prior_art_notes: Derjaguin-Landau 1941 is the Soviet-side independent derivation of what later became DLVO theory. Together with Verwey-Overbeek 1948, establishes the canonical theory of colloid stability - load-bearing for any microfluidic disclosure involving particle aggregation, cell-cell adhesion, or electrolyte-controlled microfluidic operation. Provides a 1941 anchor that predates Verwey-Overbeek by seven years.

canonical_name: Weissenberg Number Wi = gamma_dot * tau
creator: Karl Weissenberg
disclosure_citation: Weissenberg, K. (1947). 'A continuum theory of rheological phenomena.' Nature 159(4035): 310-311. doi:10.1038/159310a0
notable_capabilities: Wi = gamma_dot * tau — ratio of elastic to viscous forces in shear
high Wi: rod-climbing, normal-stress effects, elastic instabilities
essential for polymer and biomolecule on-chip rheology
prior_art_notes: Weissenberg number governs whether a viscoelastic fluid in a microchannel exhibits elastic instabilities (Pakdel-McKinley criterion: Wi sqrt(L/R) > critical). Anchors: (a) elastic-instability micromixers (passive mixing in viscoelastic solutions at low Re); (b) viscoelastic single-cell focusing (Yang 2011 and descendants); (c) polymer-solution droplet generation regime maps; (d) cell-deformability assays in polymer solutions. Any patent claim that recites 'mixing or focusing in viscoelastic fluid' is anticipated by Weissenberg-number scaling.

canonical_name: Brinkman 1947 - A calculation of the viscous force exerted by a flowing fluid on a dense swarm of particles
creator: Hendrik C. Brinkman
disclosure_citation: Brinkman, H. C. (1947). 'A calculation of the viscous force exerted by a flowing fluid on a dense swarm of particles.' Appl. Sci. Res. A1: 27-34. doi:10.1007/BF02120313
notable_capabilities: porous-medium momentum equation with viscous (Brinkman) correction term
matched-asymptotic transition between Stokes flow and Darcy flow
applicable at the porous-free-fluid interface in microfluidic devices
notes: Brinkman couples free-fluid microchannels with porous matrices - critical for hydrogel/membrane organ-on-chip theory.
prior_art_notes: Discloses the Brinkman equation: a modified Darcy law that includes a viscous diffusion term, valid for porous media of moderate-to-high permeability and at the interface between a porous region and a free-fluid channel. Anticipates patent claims involving microfluidic chambers with porous inserts (membranes, hydrogels, paper sections) bonded to open channels - the boundary condition at the interface is governed by Brinkman 1947. Load-bearing for organ-on-chip designs that pair hydrogel matrices with perfusion channels, and for membrane-on-chip immunoassays with adjacent open channels.

canonical_name: Verwey & Overbeek 1948 - Theory of the Stability of Lyophobic Colloids
creator: Evert Verwey; Theodoor Overbeek
disclosure_citation: Verwey, E. J. W., Overbeek, J. T. G. (1948). 'Theory of the Stability of Lyophobic Colloids.' Elsevier, Amsterdam.
notable_capabilities: DLVO theory of colloid stability: balance of van der Waals attraction and electric-double-layer repulsion
quantitative criterion for colloidal aggregation
foundational for all microfluidic-particle interaction theory
notes: DLVO theory anchor; pairs with Derjaguin-Landau 1941.
prior_art_notes: Verwey-Overbeek 1948 (together with Derjaguin-Landau 1941) established DLVO theory: colloid stability emerges from a balance of attractive van der Waals and repulsive electric-double-layer interactions. Anticipates microfluidic claims involving bead aggregation in on-chip immunoassays, cell-cell adhesion in droplet encapsulation, particle deposition on channel walls, and electrolyte-controlled colloid handling. Any patent claiming a 'novel colloid-stability-controlled microfluidic operation' must clear DLVO theory.
sources: Verwey, Overbeek 'Theory of the Stability of Lyophobic Colloids' Elsevier (1948)

canonical_name: The motion and precipitation of suspensoids in divergent electric fields (dielectrophoresis foundation)
creator: H. A. Pohl
disclosure_citation: Pohl, H. A. The motion and precipitation of suspensoids in divergent electric fields. J. Appl. Phys. 1951, 22, 869–871. DOI: 10.1063/1.1700065
prior_art_notes: Foundational disclosure of dielectrophoresis (DEP): the motion of polarizable particles in non-uniform electric fields, distinct from electrophoresis (which moves charged particles in uniform fields). Predates microfluidics by 40 years. Anticipates: the entire DEP-on-chip subfield (Gascoyne, Voldman, Pethig). Critical because much later DEP-on-chip disclosure can be reduced in scope by reaching back to Pohl for the foundational physics.
sources: Pohl, H. A. Dielectrophoresis. Cambridge UP 1978 (book-length treatment)

canonical_name: Taylor-Aris dispersion in pipe flow
creator: G. I. Taylor (Cambridge), R. Aris
disclosure_citation: Taylor, G. Dispersion of soluble matter in solvent flowing slowly through a tube. Proc. R. Soc. London Ser. A 1953, 219, 186–203. DOI: 10.1098/rspa.1953.0139 (and Aris, R. Proc. R. Soc. London Ser. A 1956, 235, 67–77.)
prior_art_notes: Foundational disclosure of Taylor-Aris dispersion: in pressure-driven (Poiseuille) flow through a tube, the parabolic velocity profile combined with cross-stream diffusion produces an effective axial dispersion coefficient that grows with Pe². This phenomenon is the dominant peak-broadening mechanism in chip CE and continuous-flow analysis, and the reason electroosmotic flow (with its plug-like profile) gives sharper peaks than pressure-driven flow. Anticipates: every CE chip's optimization of peak resolution by minimizing Taylor-Aris dispersion through plug-flow (electroosmotic, electrokinetic) regimes.
sources: Proc. R. Soc. London Ser. A 1953, 219, 186–203
Aris, R. Proc. R. Soc. London Ser. A 1956, 235, 67–77

canonical_name: Coulter Principle (1953 Patent) Public Domain Status Analysis
creator: Wallace H. Coulter (Coulter Electronics, later Beckman Coulter)
disclosure_citation: US2656508 (Wallace H. Coulter, granted 1953-10-20, expired 1971-10-20); existing entry coulter-1953-impedance-cell-counting-patent
notable_capabilities: foundational impedance-based particle counting
fully expired and in the public domain since 1971
anchors any modern impedance cytometry implementation as non-novel
notes: 55 years public domain as of 2026. Anchors invalidity defense for any broad impedance-cytometry assertion. Categorized as `corpus: academic` (public-domain status captured in `ip_status`).
prior_art_notes: Defensive entry. Wallace Coulter's original 1953 patent US2656508 covers the basic Coulter principle: passing a particle suspension through a small aperture between two electrolyte chambers and measuring the transient impedance change as each particle passes. The patent was granted 1953-10-20 and expired 1971-10-20 under then-applicable 17-year US patent terms. As of 2026, this technology has been in the US public domain for 55 years. Any party attempting to assert claims to (a) impedance-based particle counting; (b) aperture-based single-cell impedance measurement; (c) electrolyte-flanked sensing-volume detection — without distinguishing limitations — must overcome 55 years of public-domain prior art rooted in this patent. Companion existing entry coulter-1953-impedance-cell-counting-patent. Defensive value: this entry timestamps the public-domain status as a citable defense against any modern impedance-cytometry assertion.
sources: Coulter, Proceedings of the National Electronics Conference 1956

canonical_name: Yosioka & Kawasima 1955 - Acoustic radiation pressure on a compressible sphere
creator: Kyosuke Yosioka; Yasuhiko Kawasima
disclosure_citation: Yosioka, K., Kawasima, Y. (1955). 'Acoustic radiation pressure on a compressible sphere.' Acta Acustica united with Acustica 5(3): 167-173.
notable_capabilities: extends King 1934 to compressible spheres (cells, droplets, deformable particles)
load-bearing for cell-vs-cell acoustofluidic separation by compressibility contrast
precursor to Gorkov 1962 closed-form potential
notes: Compressible-sphere extension of King 1934.
prior_art_notes: Yosioka-Kawasima 1955 extends King 1934 from rigid to compressible spheres, essential for biological particles (cells, vesicles, droplets) whose acoustic contrast depends on both density and compressibility. Anticipates acoustofluidic claims that exploit compressibility-contrast separations (cell-from-droplet, lipid-vs-water vesicles, RBC-vs-WBC sorting) - the underlying acoustic-contrast theory is in this 1955 paper.

canonical_name: Womersley 1955 — Womersley Number alpha for Pulsatile Flow
creator: John Ronald Womersley
disclosure_citation: Womersley, J. R. (1955). 'Method for the calculation of velocity, rate of flow and viscous drag in arteries when the pressure gradient is known.' Journal of Physiology 127(3): 553-563. doi:10.1113/jphysiol.1955.sp005276
notable_capabilities: alpha = R sqrt(omega rho / mu) — ratio of unsteady to viscous forces
controls velocity profile in pulsatile flow (Womersley vs Poiseuille parabolic)
essential for biomimetic arterial-flow on-chip models
prior_art_notes: Womersley number anchors all pulsatile-flow microfluidic devices used in vascular-on-chip and arterial-flow modeling. At alpha ~ 1, viscous and unsteady inertia balance and the velocity profile differs significantly from steady Poiseuille. Anticipates: (a) endothelial-cell-on-chip platforms that recite physiologic pulsatile shear; (b) pulsatile organ-on-chip perfusion modules; (c) arterial-disease drug-screening chips that depend on pulsatile mass-transfer. Any patent claim to 'physiologic pulsatile shear in a microchannel' is anticipated by the Womersley group together with the Womersley 1955 derivation.

canonical_name: Aris 1956 — On the dispersion of a solute in a fluid flowing through a tube (Aris extension to Taylor dispersion)
creator: Rutherford Aris
disclosure_citation: R. Aris, 'On the dispersion of a solute in a fluid flowing through a tube', Proc. Roy. Soc. A 235, 67-77 (1956); doi:10.1098/rspa.1956.0065
prior_art_notes: Aris's mathematical extension of Taylor's 1953 dispersion analysis to arbitrary cross-sections and to the asymptotic-time regime, giving the canonical 'Taylor-Aris dispersion coefficient' D_eff = D + Pe^2 D / 192 (for circular tube). Anticipates: any microfluidic patent that exploits or claims to mitigate hydrodynamic dispersion in a channel — the Taylor-Aris coefficient is the standard reference value, 70 years old. Critical to chip-CE, chip-HPLC, and any continuous-flow on-chip reactor where peak broadening matters.

canonical_name: Saffman & Taylor 1958 — The penetration of a fluid into a porous medium or Hele-Shaw cell containing a more viscous liquid (viscous fingering)
creator: Philip Geoffrey Saffman, Geoffrey Ingram Taylor
disclosure_citation: P.G. Saffman, G.I. Taylor, 'The penetration of a fluid into a porous medium or Hele-Shaw cell containing a more viscous liquid', Proc. Roy. Soc. A 245, 312-329 (1958); doi:10.1098/rspa.1958.0085
prior_art_notes: Foundational analysis of the interfacial instability when a less-viscous fluid displaces a more-viscous fluid in a Hele-Shaw cell or porous medium. Anticipates: microfluidic patents claiming 'controlled fingering for emulsion generation', 'pattern formation in microchannels', or 'porous-media-on-chip' devices — the underlying instability and its scaling are 68 years old. Critical reference for any displacement-flow microfluidic patent (chip-based EOR studies, blood-plasma separation by displacement, etc.).

canonical_name: Bird, Stewart & Lightfoot 1960 - Transport Phenomena (textbook, 1st ed.)
creator: R. Byron Bird; Warren E. Stewart; Edwin N. Lightfoot
disclosure_citation: Bird, R. B., Stewart, W. E., Lightfoot, E. N. (1960). 'Transport Phenomena.' John Wiley & Sons, New York. ISBN 978-0-471-07392-5.
notable_capabilities: unified treatment of momentum, heat, and mass transport
Newton-Fourier-Fick analogy as the organizing principle
reference textbook for every microfluidic theory paper since 1960
notes: Single most-cited textbook in microfluidic theory; required anchor for any transport-novelty claim.
prior_art_notes: Bird-Stewart-Lightfoot is the foundational textbook for transport phenomena, presenting the unified Newton-Fourier-Fick framework that underlies every microfluidic transport calculation. The 1960 edition documents laminar Navier-Stokes solutions for ducts of every cross-section, Taylor dispersion (chapter on solute transport), heat transfer in channels, and mass transfer with chemical reaction. Anticipates any patent claim whose novel transport formula reduces to a textbook BSL relation - laminar parabolic profile in a channel, Hagen-Poiseuille for any duct section, Graetz-Nusselt for thermal entry length, Leveque mass-transfer correlation. BSL is the single most-cited textbook in microfluidic theory; any transport-theory novelty must clear it.

canonical_name: Bretherton 1961 - The motion of long bubbles in tubes
creator: Francis P. Bretherton
disclosure_citation: Bretherton, F. P. (1961). 'The motion of long bubbles in tubes.' J. Fluid Mech. 10(2): 166-188. doi:10.1017/S0022112061000160
notable_capabilities: closed-form thickness law h/R ~ 1.34 Ca^(2/3) for the lubricating film between a long bubble and the channel wall
capillary-number scaling of bubble velocity vs liquid bulk velocity
pressure drop across a moving bubble in a capillary
notes: Classical anchor for any segmented-flow or Taylor-flow microfluidic disclosure.
prior_art_notes: Discloses the canonical scaling for a confined-bubble system: thin liquid film thickness, bubble velocity offset from mean flow, and capillary pressure drop across the bubble - all functions of Ca = mu*U/gamma. Anticipates microfluidic claims involving Taylor-flow segmented gas-liquid reactors, bubble-trains in segmented-flow microreactors, on-chip oxygenation, gas-liquid heat-exchange microchannels, and bubble-based mixing enhancement claims keyed to film-thickness control. Any patent that claims a quantitative relationship between bubble velocity and channel film thickness, or that uses Ca^(2/3) scaling to predict performance, is anticipated by Bretherton 1961.

canonical_name: Vroman effect: time-resolved competitive protein adsorption
creator: Leo Vroman
disclosure_citation: Vroman, L. Effect of adsorbed proteins on the wettability of hydrophilic and hydrophobic solids. Nature 1962, 196, 476–477. DOI: 10.1038/196476a0
prior_art_notes: Foundational disclosure of the Vroman effect: when blood or serum contacts a surface, smaller proteins adsorb first and are subsequently displaced by larger proteins in a kinetic cascade ending with high-molecular-weight kininogen on most surfaces. Critical context for any blood-contacting microfluidic device — protein fouling on surfaces is essentially impossible to prevent without active passivation. Doctrinally relevant for invalidity contention against patents claiming 'novel non-fouling surface' that turns out to be a known passivation chemistry.

canonical_name: Boyden chamber chemotaxis assay
creator: Stephen Boyden
disclosure_citation: Boyden, S. The chemotactic effect of mixtures of antibody and antigen on polymorphonuclear leucocytes. J. Exp. Med. 1962, 115, 453–466. DOI: 10.1084/jem.115.3.453
prior_art_notes: The Boyden chamber: two compartments separated by a porous membrane (typ. 5 µm pore polycarbonate) with chemoattractant in the lower compartment and cells in the upper compartment. Cells migrate through the membrane in proportion to chemoattractant gradient. Microfluidic-relevant prior art: every microfluidic chemotaxis chip (gradient generator + cell observation chamber) is conceptually downstream of the Boyden chamber. Anticipates: porous-membrane-separated-chamber architecture for cell migration assays.

canonical_name: Gorkov 1962 - Forces acting on a small particle in an acoustical field in an ideal fluid
creator: Lev P. Gorkov
disclosure_citation: Gorkov, L. P. (1962). 'On the forces acting on a small particle in an acoustical field in an ideal fluid.' Soviet Physics Doklady 6: 773-775.
notable_capabilities: closed-form acoustic radiation potential for small particles
Gorkov potential U = (V*pa^2/(4*rho_f*c_f^2))*f1 - (3*V*rho_f*va^2/8)*f2
universal expression used in every modern acoustofluidic design
notes: Gorkov potential is the universal modern expression for acoustic radiation force.
prior_art_notes: Gorkov 1962 derives the closed-form acoustic-radiation-potential expression for small particles (a << lambda) in an arbitrary acoustic field. The Gorkov potential is the load-bearing relation for designing modern acoustofluidic devices: BAW separation chips, SAW-based cell-sorters, acoustic-tweezers. Anticipates patent claims reciting acoustic-field design for particle trapping or sorting - the underlying potential expression is from 1962. Particularly load-bearing for the entire acoustofluidic patent ecosystem (Sirius/Erbi Bio/Acoustics-Inside/Folch group portfolios).

canonical_name: Segre & Silberberg 1962 - Behaviour of macroscopic rigid spheres in Poiseuille flow
creator: Gershon Segre; Alexander Silberberg
disclosure_citation: Segre, G., Silberberg, A. (1962). 'Behaviour of macroscopic rigid spheres in Poiseuille flow. Part 2.' J. Fluid Mech. 14(1): 136-157. doi:10.1017/S0022112062001111. Companion: Segre-Silberberg, Nature 189, 209 (1961).
notable_capabilities: discovery of the tubular-pinch effect: rigid particles in laminar pipe flow migrate to an annulus at ~0.6 of the pipe radius
inertial-lift force balance against shear-gradient force
foundational for ALL inertial-focusing microfluidic devices
notes: The foundational anchor for ALL inertial-focusing microfluidic patents.
prior_art_notes: Segre-Silberberg 1961-1962 is the foundational experimental paper documenting the tubular-pinch effect: rigid spheres in laminar pipe flow at finite Re migrate to an equilibrium radial position. Anticipates the entire inertial-focusing microfluidic ecosystem: Di Carlo group spiral inertial focusing, sheath-free flow cytometry, particle-sorting-by-inertial-equilibrium-position, and every patent reciting 'particles focused to an equilibrium streamline by inertia' (Di Carlo, Vortex Bio, Forte Bio, Velocyto). 60 years of microfluidic inertial focusing reduces to Segre-Silberberg.

canonical_name: Karnis & Mason 1963 - Particle migration in Poiseuille flow
creator: Andrew Karnis; Stanley G. Mason
disclosure_citation: Karnis, A., Mason, S. G. (1963). 'Particle motions in sheared suspensions: XXIII. Wall migration of fluid drops.' J. Colloid Sci. 18: 257-281.
notable_capabilities: systematic experimental study of particle/drop migration in shear and Poiseuille flow
wall-migration of deformable drops in tubes
companion-anchor to Segre-Silberberg for inertial migration
notes: Companion to Segre-Silberberg; covers deformable drops and wall migration.
prior_art_notes: Karnis-Mason 1963 systematically documents particle and drop migration in Poiseuille and shear flow, including wall-migration of deformable drops. Anticipates droplet-focusing microfluidic claims keyed on drop deformability, cell-sorting by deformability in inertial channels (Di Carlo deformability cytometry), and any 'cross-stream migration' patent for cells or droplets in laminar tube flow. Companion to Segre-Silberberg 1962.

canonical_name: Taylor 1964 - Disintegration of water drops in an electric field (Taylor cone)
creator: Sir Geoffrey Ingram Taylor
disclosure_citation: Taylor, G. I. (1964). 'Disintegration of water drops in an electric field.' Proc. R. Soc. A 280(1382): 383-397. doi:10.1098/rspa.1964.0151
notable_capabilities: Taylor cone half-angle (~49.3 degrees) at the threshold of conical-jet emission
theory of electrified drop disintegration under uniform field
foundational for electrospray and electrohydrodynamic microfluidics
notes: Taylor cone - foundational anchor for ALL electrospray microfluidics.
prior_art_notes: Taylor 1964 derives the conical interface (Taylor cone) of a charged-fluid meniscus at the verge of jet emission. Foundational paper for electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (the Fenn 1989 prize-winning method), electrohydrodynamic droplet generation on chip, electrospinning of polymer fibers via microfluidic emitters, and Taylor-cone microfluidic emitter arrays for mass-spectrometry interfacing. Anticipates any patent claim reciting 'conical electrified meniscus emitting a jet at a threshold voltage' or 'electrospray emitter integrated with microfluidic chip'.

canonical_name: Deborah Number De = tau / T (Reiner 1964)
creator: Markus Reiner
disclosure_citation: Reiner, M. (1964). 'The Deborah Number.' Physics Today 17(1): 62. doi:10.1063/1.3051374
notable_capabilities: De = tau_relaxation / T_observation — ratio of fluid relaxation time to observation time
De >> 1: solid-like elastic response; De << 1: liquid-like viscous response
complements Weissenberg number for viscoelastic flow characterization
prior_art_notes: Deborah number anchors viscoelastic microfluidics: any chip that handles polymer solutions, biopolymer solutions, mucus, blood, or DNA solutions with significant relaxation time operates at finite De and exhibits non-Newtonian flow features (elastic instabilities, secondary flows, viscoelastic focusing). Anticipates: (a) elasto-inertial focusing patents; (b) DNA-stretching-on-chip patents; (c) viscoelastic-focusing single-cell platforms; (d) DEAN-flow vortex generators in viscoelastic fluids.

canonical_name: Continuous inkjet (Sweet 1965)
creator: Richard Sweet (Stanford)
disclosure_citation: Sweet, R. G. High-frequency recording with electrostatically deflected ink jets. Rev. Sci. Instrum. 1965, 36, 131–136. DOI: 10.1063/1.1719502
